newsitem.title: USA: Allies told decision not final on Cuba law.
newsitem.headline: Allies told decision not final on Cuba law.

text.p: The United States, in an appeal to angry European allies, on Tuesday stressed that a final decision has not been made on whether to permit lawsuits against foreign firms operating confiscated property in Cuba.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns also faulted Europeans for viewing Cuban President Fidel Castro as a "romantic revolutionary" and for caring more about human rights in the Middle East than in the Western Hemisphere.

Under the controversial Helms-Burton law, the U.S. president in January and February 1997 "has to make a decision about one important feature of Helms-Burton and that is the ability of American citizens to sue in U.S. courts. And that hasn't been made yet," Burns told reporters.

Castro is "not a romantic revolutionary ... It's fashionable in some parts of Europe to think that he is. He is an old man who is out of touch. He's the lone autocrat in this hemisphere. Europeans ought to realise that," he said.

Burns made his comments as the spat continued between the United States and some of its closest allies over the Helms-Burton law, which stiffens and expands the 34-year-old U.S. trade embargo against communist-ruled Cuba.

President Bill Clinton's special envoy, Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat, is on another mission to Europe this week trying to persuade the allies to make common cause with Washington in pressuring Castro to make democratic, human rights and economic reforms.

Far from showing any interest in working with the United States on this issue, however, European Union foreign ministers retaliated by approving on Monday a law that would make it illegal for Europeans to obey Washington's anti-Cuba Helms-Burton Act.

The Helms-Burton law allows lawsuits to be filed in U.S. courts against foreign firms that own or operate properties seized by Cuba from U.S. citizens who were Cuban nationals before the 1959 communist revolution.
Last July Clinton ordered the sanctions to come into force but delayed implementation for six months to appease U.S. allies who threatened retaliation.

The law also allows denial of visas to shareholders and officers of foreign firms operating these properties in Cuba and this provision has already been used to punish a Canadian mining company and a Mexican telecommunications firm.
Burns stressed that delaying implementation of the lawsuits was a gesture to Europe, Mexico and Canada -- key allies affected by the law.

But ahead of a final decision about whether the lawsuits will be allowed to go forward, "We need a little help from the Europeans ... It would be very helpful if they showed a little bit of concern for the victims of Fidel Castro," he said.

Europeans "are champions of human rights in many parts of the world. And they are very quick to talk about human rights violations in Asia and Africa, in the Middle East ... It would be interesting to hear that, and useful, about the major human rights violator in the Western Hemisphere, Fidel Castro."

While the Helms-Burton Act outraged Washington's closest allies and main trade partners, it helped solidify Clinton's political support among Cuban-Americans, many of whom live in Florida, a crucial state in the Nov. 5 presidential election.
